edition.locus: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia (archive bub_gb_DY2xvRwPetMC), Latin column, chapter III, printed p. 44 (PDF page 68)

source_text: Quod porro Anima sit substantia, sic ostenditur: Primo quidem, quoniam illi quoque definitio substantiae iure convenit, quae quidem est eiusmodi: Substantia est id, quod cum unum et idem sit numero, contraria vicissim suscipit. Quod vero Anima a natura propria non recedens, contraria vicissim suscipiat, omnibus credo est perspicuum. Iustitia enim et iniustitia, fortitudo et timiditas, temperantia et intemperantia, in ipsa vicissim cernuntur, quum sint contraria. Quamobrem cum ea substantiae sit proprietas, ut contrariorum vicissim susceptrix sit, eademque Animae conveniat; substantia igitur anima erit. Praeterea, cum et corpus sit substantia, Animam quoque substantiam esse necesse est. Neque enim fieri potest, ut quod vitam accipit, substantia sit; illud autem quod vitam praebet, non sit substantia. Nisi forte quis ita insaniat, ut id quod non est, eius quod est, causam esse affirmet: aut rursus id, cuius illud ipsum quod est, ex alio sic pendet, ut absque illo esse nequeat, eius, ipsius, ex quo pendet, causam esse velit.
thought_title: That the soul is a substance
orientation: The soul fits the definition of substance, since it stays one and the same while receiving opposite qualities such as justice and injustice; and what gives life to the body, itself a substance, must also be a substance.
pass_a_gloss: That moreover (porro) the soul is a substance (substantia) is shown (ostenditur) thus. First, because to it also the definition (definitio) of substance rightly (iure) fits (convenit), which is of this kind: substance is that which, while it is one and the same in number (unum et idem numero), receives (suscipit) contraries (contraria) in turn (vicissim). That the soul, not departing (non recedens) from its own nature (natura propria), receives contraries in turn is, I believe, clear (perspicuum) to all. For justice and injustice (iustitia et iniustitia), courage and timidity (fortitudo et timiditas), temperance and intemperance (temperantia et intemperantia) are discerned (cernuntur) in it in turn, since they are contraries. Wherefore, since this is the property (proprietas) of substance, that it be a receiver (susceptrix) of contraries in turn, and the same fits the soul, the soul therefore will be a substance. Besides (praeterea), since the body too is a substance, the soul also must (necesse est) be a substance. For it cannot happen that what receives (accipit) life is a substance, but that which furnishes (praebet) life is not a substance. Unless perhaps someone is so insane (insaniat) as to affirm that that which is not (quod non est) is the cause (causam) of that which is (quod est); or again would have that thing, whose very being (illud ipsum quod est) so hangs (pendet) from another that it cannot be without it, to be the cause of that very thing from which it hangs.

pass_b_english: Further, that the soul is a substance is shown as follows. First, because the definition of substance rightly fits it as well. That definition runs like this: a substance is that which, while remaining one and the same in number, receives contraries in turn. That the soul, without departing from its own nature, receives contraries in turn is plain to everyone, I think. For justice and injustice, courage and cowardice, temperance and intemperance are seen in it by turns, and these are contraries. Since it is the property of substance to receive contraries in turn, and this same property belongs to the soul, the soul will therefore be a substance.

Moreover, since the body is a substance, the soul too must be a substance. For it cannot be that what receives life is a substance, while what gives life is not a substance, unless perhaps someone is so mad as to claim that what is not is the cause of what is; or again, to hold that a thing whose very being so depends on another that it cannot exist without it is the cause of the very thing on which it depends.
notes: Edition chapter III ('An Anima sit substantia').
The definition of substance (one and the same in number, receiving contraries) is Aristotle's (Categories 5, 4a10); a philosophical source, not Scripture, so nothing is cited in the text.
The printed 'eius, ipsius, ex quo pendet' is read as 'of that very thing on which it depends', as the source note gives.
'timiditas' rendered 'cowardice' as the contrary of courage.
One Latin paragraph split into two English paragraphs at 'Praeterea' (the second argument).
